newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Protesters, dogs take Serbia police by surprise.
newsitem.headline: Protesters, dogs take Serbia police by surprise.

text.p: Thousands of anti-government protesters took Serbia's feared security forces by surprise when they jammed Belgrade city centre late on Sunday after a noisy dog-led demonstration earlier in the day.

Supporters of the opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition had trotted out a new strategy for the 63rd consecutive day of street protests, getting hundreds of pet dogs to walk -- and sometimes bark -- for democracy.

Hours after Zajedno's main rally ended, thousands of people took to the streets again in support of students who are mounting their own separate protests against the government's annulment of opposition victories in municipal elections.
They confronted the only remaining police cordon in the city centre after scores of busloads of police had left believing the day's demonstration was over.
Hundreds of students, many with candles in their hands, faced off against the police with a large cross and an icon they said came from the holy Serbian town of Chilandar in Greece.

Hundreds of dogs had joined their masters on the streets earlier. Great danes, bulldogs, poodles, cocker spaniels, Irish setters, rottweilers, dalmatians and chihuahuas added canine cacophony to the usual din of whistles, drums and chants.
Some of the dogs looked flustered from all the racket while others joined in heartily, barking at riot police trying to enforce a ban on street marches.
Nine weeks of Zajedno demonstrations have been distinctive for non-violence, creativity and humour and the rally of the dogs was no exception.

But autocratic President Slobodan Milosevic and his Socialist Party have shown no sign of willingness to accept all opposition victories in Serbia's November 17 municipal elections, as demanded by Zajedno and the West.

An OSCE investigation dismissed the Socialist claim of unspecified "irregularities" in the elections and verified that Zajedno won majorities in 14 towns and cities including the two biggest, Belgrade and Nis.

With the West warning Milosevic to respect democratic principles or forget about aid for Serbia's wrecked economy, Socialist-led electoral commissions admitted last week that Zajedno did win in Belgrade and Nis.
Heartened Zajedno activists said they would convene the new local assembly in Nis on January 27 after a municipal court rejected an appeal by hardline Socialists against the commission verdict.
But some political analysts predicted that Socialist diehards could still retain control of local governments through state-manipulated higher courts and bureaucratic obstruction.
Moreover, ethnic violence in Serbia's Albanian-majority province of Kosovo could allow Milosevic to distract attention from the elections issue and reassert the appeal of strong Socialist leadership.

State-run mainstream media jumped on allegations by the Serb Socialist mayor of Pristina in Kosovo that Zajedno was involved in a car bombing that gravely injured the Serb rector of the city's university last week.

Zajedno condemned the bomb attack and denied any connection with it, accusing neo-communists close to Milosevic of trying to provoke an anti-Albanian backlash and emergency rule which could suppress any anti-government protests.

"Last night's state TV news shows without a shadow of a doubt that Milosevic is now playing his last card -- provoke a bloodbath in Kosovo to divert all attention from the election," Zajedno co-leader Vuk Draskovic told the rally in Belgrade.
"In his madness he is not even thinking what that would mean for Serbia -- new international sanctions. The whole world will be against us again."
